instruction: Why do I have to wear this bracelet on my arm?
response: That bracelet is really important! It has your name and birthday on it, plus a special barcode. Before anyone gives you medicine or does a test, they check your bracelet to make absolutely sure they have the right person. Think of it like a VIP pass that tells everyone exactly who you are so they can take the best care of you.

instruction: What is the SMILE Room?
response: The SMILE Room is a super cool room on the sixth floor that's full of things to help you relax or have fun! It has bubble columns with colours moving inside them, fibre optic lights you can touch, mirrors, and music. It's a special place where you can go to feel calm or just enjoy some really neat sensory stuff. You can ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you'd like to visit!

instruction: Is there a playground here?
response: There isn't an outdoor playground, but there are some awesome rooms to play in! There's Ashley's Backyard on the sixth floor, which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids, and there's also a School-Age Activity Room where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and work on puzzles. A grown-up just needs to come with you. Ask your nurse which one you can visit!

instruction: Can my dog come visit me?
response: Regular pet visits aren't allowed at the hospital because they want to keep all the kids here safe and healthy. But guess what — sometimes therapy dogs from St. John Ambulance come to visit patients! Those are specially trained dogs that are really gentle. You can ask your care team if a therapy dog visit is coming up soon. That would be pretty exciting, right?

instruction: What are Bravery Beads?
response: Bravery Beads are so cool! Every time something happens during your care — like a test, a treatment, or a procedure — you get a special bead to put on a string. Each kind of bead means something different. Over time, you build this amazing collection that tells the story of how brave you've been. It's like a necklace or keychain that shows everything you've been through. Ask your care team if you'd like to start collecting them!

instruction: Who is Ollie?
response: Ollie is the hospital's very own therapeutic clown! Ollie's whole job is to help kids laugh, play, and have fun while they're in the hospital. Ollie is specially trained to make your day a little brighter and help things feel more normal. If you see Ollie around, you're in for a treat!

instruction: Why does everyone keep washing their hands so much?
response: Great question! Germs are tiny things that are way too small to see, and they can make people sick. In the hospital, washing hands is the number one way to stop germs from spreading from one person to another. That's why your nurses, doctors, and even your visitors clean their hands every time they come into your room and every time they leave. You can help too by washing your hands — especially before you eat!

instruction: Can I watch TV?
response: Yes! The hospital has a special entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free. And if your family has a streaming service like Netflix or Disney+, you can log in with your own account and watch that too. Ask your nurse to help you get it set up if you're not sure how!

instruction: What does the person in the white coat do?
response: People in white coats are usually doctors, but sometimes they might be medical students who are still learning to become doctors! They work as a team. The main doctor is called the attending physician, and they're in charge of your care. If a younger person in a white coat comes to check on you, they might be a student or a resident — that's someone who finished medical school and is getting extra training. They all work together to help you feel better.

instruction: Where does my food come from in the hospital?
response: The hospital has its own kitchen called Patient Food Services! They make breakfast, lunch, and dinner for all the patients. Your doctor picks a menu that's right for you, and then you get a form on your breakfast tray where you can choose what you'd like to eat the next day. Breakfast comes in the morning, lunch around noon, and dinner in the late afternoon. If your family wants a snack, there's a Tim Hortons on the second floor too!

instruction: What exactly is a Care Partner and how is that different from a regular visitor?
response: At Children's Hospital, a Care Partner is someone who's actively involved in supporting your care — usually a parent or guardian. They have more access than regular visitors. For inpatients, up to two Care Partners can be at your bedside at a time, while outpatients are allowed one. Regular visitors follow more general visiting guidelines based on the unit and your condition. During outbreaks or COVID precautions, only essential Care Partners are permitted, and regular visiting may be restricted. Care Partners don't need to register currently, but they're encouraged to wear a mask at all times.

instruction: How does the weapons detection system work when I go to the emergency department?
response: LHSC uses an advanced screening system at the entrances to the Emergency Department. It's non-invasive, meaning you just walk through without stopping or emptying your pockets. The technology is designed to detect potential threats like weapons. If something flags, a trained security guard may check your belongings. Everyone entering the ED goes through it, including minors accompanied by a parent or guardian. If you need accommodations for any reason, you can speak to the security guard at the entrance before going through.

instruction: I'm bored out of my mind. Is there a way to connect with other teens who are also stuck in the hospital?
response: There's actually a platform for that called Upopolis. It's a free, secure social networking site specifically for paediatric patients aged 8 to 18 across Canada. You can connect with other young people who are also going through hospital stays, which can help it feel a lot less isolating. Laptops are available through Child Life Services if you need one. Ask a Child Life Specialist to get you set up — they can walk you through how it works.

instruction: What's the deal with the room numbering system here? I keep getting lost.
response: The room numbers follow a specific format that's actually pretty logical once you decode it. Take B2-503 as an example: the letter tells you the zone (B), the first number is the floor (2), and 503 is the actual room number. So that room is in Zone B, second floor, room 503. The hospital also has a free app called MazeMap where you can search the Victoria Hospital map. You can also scan QR codes on posters near the elevators to pull up directions while you're on-site.

instruction: Can I use my phone in the hospital?
response: Yes, you're actually encouraged to use your own cell phone to make calls and stay in touch with friends and family. The hospital also has patient telephones available for local and toll-free calls at no cost. For internet access, there's WiFi available — if you run into any issues connecting, there's a Data Valet helpline you can call. You can also use your phone to access the patient entertainment site for streaming if you have your own account.

instruction: I speak French at home. Can I get information or talk to someone in French here?
response: Absolutely. LHSC provides free interpretation services for patients, and that includes French. You can ask your care team to arrange for an interpreter so you can communicate comfortably during appointments and discussions about your care. The Patient Relations contact form is also available in French on the LHSC website. Let your nurse or anyone on your care team know your preference, and they'll make the arrangements.

instruction: What's the Paediatric Family Resource Centre? My mom mentioned it but I didn't really get what it is.
response: It's basically a support hub for patients and families located on the first floor of Zone B, room B1-006. They offer peer support from people who have lived experience, help with filling out forms and applications, and access to information about different children's health topics. There's also internet access there. It's open most weekdays and has limited weekend hours by appointment. It's a good spot if you or your family need help navigating things or just want a quieter space to look up information.

instruction: Why does the hospital not allow latex balloons? That seems kind of random.
response: It's actually a safety thing. Some people have serious latex allergies, and latex balloons can trigger severe allergic reactions — not just from touching them, but even from particles in the air when they pop. In a hospital full of vulnerable patients, that's a real risk. Interestingly, poinsettia plants are also banned here for a similar reason — they contain a compound chemically similar to rubber latex. So it's not random at all; it's about protecting everyone in the building, especially patients with compromised immune systems.

instruction: What happens during a bedside shift change? The nurses keep inviting me to participate but I don't know what that means.
response: A bedside shift change report is when the nurse finishing their shift hands off your care information to the nurse starting the next shift — and they do it right at your bedside instead of behind closed doors. It usually takes about three to five minutes. The incoming nurse will introduce themselves, they'll go over your plan of care together, run through some safety checks, and then ask if you have any questions or anything to add. It's a chance for you to hear exactly what's happening with your care and correct anything that doesn't sound right. You can participate as much or as little as you want.

instruction: I heard there's a Gender Pathways Service here. What does that actually involve?
response: The Gender Pathways Service, or GPS, provides gender-affirming care to gender diverse and transgender children and adolescents aged 17 and under. It's a multidisciplinary service, meaning it brings together professionals from different specialties. The program follows established North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. If you're interested in learning more or accessing the service, you can reach them at gps@lhsc.on.ca or ask your care team to connect you.
